newsitem.title: UK: Lustreless gold tumbles to 18-month lows.
newsitem.headline: Lustreless gold tumbles to 18-month lows.

text.p: Gold prices slid to 18-month lows on Tuesday amid overwhelmingly bearish market sentiment, and analysts said it still had room to fall further.
"People are trying to get gold lower and there's been some substantial selling around," an analyst said.
Gold shed about $2 overnight and fixed at $377.05 an ounce in the morning, the lowest level since March 6, 1995.
It recovered modestly in the afternoon, however, to close at $378.65, virtually unchanged from Monday's weak finish.
Gold started crumbling badly last week when investment funds became impatient with its apparent lack of profit potential compared with booming stock and bond markets.
The strong dollar has helped squeeze speculative money out of the precious metals by further discouraging already disillusioned investors.
"The dollar's been strong, interest rates low and stocks and bonds markets looking good. There's been every good reason to put money in other markets," a dealer said.
The dollar's strength against the yen, which hit a 2-1/2 year high on Monday, and a sluggish Japanese economy were playing a role in the malaise affecting precious metals.
"The latest Japanese import figures showed gold import figures in the first half of the year at nearly half of their 1995 levels," brokers GNI Ltd said in a daily commentary.

Platinum also gave up ground to fix at a near-two-year low of $381.50 an ounce, the lowest fixing since January 28, 1994. But it firmed with gold and finished $1.00 firmer than Monday at $384.25 an ounce.
Silver closed at $4.91, up four cents, while palladium ended $0.75 firmer at $119.50.

Gold is just the latest commodity to take a hit. September saw most commodity prices -- with the notable exception of oil -- suffer from weak end-user demand and dwindling speculative interest as equities and bonds boomed.
Benchmark North Sea crude oil futures are at their strongest since the 1991 Gulf War, above $23 per barrel on new Middle East tension and demand for heating fuel to replenish low stocks.

But, like bullion, industrial metals sank when demand failed to live up to seasonal expectations. Aluminium is at its lowest for 2-1/4 years around $1,380 per tonne. Brokerage GNI Ltd also cited the strong dollar as the culprit in the latest falls, saying it had deterred Asian buyers who had been out bargain-hunting for aluminium. Grain prices earlier this year more than matched the rally in crude oil. In March, after drought depressed world stocks to the lowest since the 1970s, the nearby Chicago wheat contract "spiked" to a record $7.50 per bushel. Predictions of bigger crops have taken the heat out of the rally, however, and CBOT wheat is now at $4.30.
